name: Imprezia
tagline: AI tool that turns a prompt or a pile of notes into a finished-looking presentation.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The generation half of this is genuinely easy: an LLM is good at turning a topic into an outline, and an outline into slide markup is a solved problem with Reveal.js or Marp. An agent can wire that up in a sitting and give you a local CLI that spits out an HTML deck and a PDF. The part that does not come free is taste: consistent type scale, layouts that do not break when a bullet runs long, charts, images that match the topic, and an export that survives being opened in PowerPoint by someone else. Expect your version to look like a competent developer's deck, which is a real category and not always the one you want. If the deck is for you, build it; if it is for a client who will reopen and edit it in Google Slides, buy the thing.
coreLoopDIY: A local CLI that takes a topic or a notes file, asks an LLM for a structured slide outline, and renders it into a themed HTML deck plus a PDF.
requirements: An LLM API key (OpenAI or Anthropic) in .env
Chromium via Playwright for PDF export
Willingness to hand-tune one CSS theme once
whatYouLose: Designed templates and layout variety that hold up under long text
PPTX and Google Slides export that other people can actually edit
On-theme image and chart generation instead of empty boxes
Browser editing, so every tweak is a code or markdown edit
Sharing links, view analytics, and anything collaborative
moatNotes: Deck tools live or die on whether the output looks professional at a glance and whether it opens cleanly in the format the recipient uses.
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay for deck generators for the same reason they pay for resume builders: the output is going in front of someone whose opinion matters, and 'I wrote the CSS myself' is not a feature they can see. A self-built generator nails the structure and the words, which is most of the work, and then falls over on the last ten percent that is entirely visual. Add the editing loop, where you need to nudge one slide right before a meeting without touching a template file, and the hosted product earns its money.
notes: Build it if your slides are for thinking out loud, buy it if they are a deliverable.
prompt:
Build a local command line presentation generator in an empty folder. No accounts, no server, no telemetry.

Stack, non negotiable:
- Node 20 with TypeScript, run via tsx
- Commander for the CLI
- OpenAI SDK, model and API key read from .env (OPENAI_API_KEY, OPENAI_MODEL)
- Reveal.js for rendering, loaded from a local copy in node_modules
- Playwright (chromium) for PDF export
- Zod to validate the model output

Commands:
1. `deck new "topic"` and `deck new --from notes.md` : calls the model once with a strict JSON schema and writes decks/<slug>/deck.json
2. `deck render <slug>` : renders deck.json into decks/<slug>/index.html using one theme
3. `deck pdf <slug>` : renders then prints to decks/<slug>/deck.pdf via Playwright
4. `deck serve <slug>` : static file server on localhost:5173 with live reload on deck.json change

The deck.json schema: title, subtitle, optional presenter, and a slides array. Each slide has a layout of "title" | "bullets" | "quote" | "two-column" | "section", a heading, optional body text, optional bullets (max 5, max 12 words each), and optional speakerNotes. Enforce those limits in Zod and retry the model once with the validation error appended if it fails.

Rendering rules: one handwritten CSS theme, a fixed type scale, slides that shrink text rather than overflow, speaker notes wired into the Reveal notes plugin. Ship a sensible dark theme and a light theme, selectable by flag, and nothing else.

Explicitly out of scope: image generation, charts, PPTX export, a web editor, auth, hosting, sharing links.

Include a README with setup steps, a .env.example, and one sample deck committed under decks/sample so `deck render sample` works before any API key is set.
